query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled sub–glass transition annealing treatment improves the glass‐forming ability and thermal stability of phosphorus-containing high-entropy amorphous alloys by facilitating an irreversible glass-to-glass transition that enhances short- and medium-range atomic ordering.
generation.material_initial_state: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy (e.g., Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20) in its as-quenched amorphous state produced via rapid quenching (e.g., melt-spinning).
generation.intervention: Subject the as-quenched amorphous alloy to a controlled annealing treatment at a temperature of approximately 0.8×Tg for one hour under an inert atmosphere, followed by rapid quenching to room temperature.
generation.conditions: This treatment is expected to be effective under conditions where the annealing temperature is maintained below Tg to avoid crystallization. Deviations from the target temperature or duration (e.g., significantly lower temperatures or shorter annealing times) may not sufficiently promote the necessary structural relaxation.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced short- and medium-range atomic ordering through an irreversible glass-to-glass transition that reduces internal free volume and minimizes nucleation sites.
generation.mechanism: Sub–Tg annealing facilitates subtle atomic rearrangements that lead to a denser, lower-energy amorphous configuration. This process kinetically stabilizes the structure by reducing defects and potential nucleation centers that would otherwise lead to crystallization, thereby increasing the thermal stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) should reveal an upward shift in the crystallization onset temperature and a broader supercooled liquid region, while X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) will confirm that the sample remains amorphous and exhibits enhanced medium-range ordering compared to the unannealed baseline.
generation.baseline: The as-quenched phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy before any heat treatment.
generation.boundary: This intervention is most applicable to alloys similar in composition to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 prepared via rapid quenching. It may not be effective if the applied temperature approaches or exceeds Tg, or in alloys with substantially different compositions or processing histories.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement in crystallization onset temperature and the degree of enhancement in the amorphous structure’s stability remain to be quantified experimentally. Sensitivity to precise temperature control and alloy composition variations also introduces some uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of melt-spun ribbons of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20. One set serves as the untreated baseline (as-quenched), and the other is subjected to the controlled sub-Tg annealing treatment (heating to ~0.8×Tg for one hour under argon followed by rapid quenching).
measurements: DSC to determine the crystallization onset temperature and measure the supercooled liquid region width
XRD to verify that the amorphous structure is retained post-treatment
TEM to assess changes in medium-range ordering and detect any signs of crystallization
Potential free-volume measurements to evaluate atomic densification
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in the crystallization onset temperature and the supercooled liquid region, or if evidence of crystallization appears in XRD or TEM analyses compared to the untreated baseline, then the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.kind: web:The glass-to-glass transition and the glass structures of the HEMG
cited_evidence.text: Synchrotron X-ray diffraction results show that the heat-treated sample possesses an amorphous structure, but its G(r) (heat-treated curve in Fig. 1d) at room temperature is quite different from that of the as-prepared sample. Specifically, the intensity maximum moves from the left side (as-prepared curve in Fig. 1d) to the right side (heat-treated curve in Fig. 1d) of the first peak in G(r). Moreover, a clearer peak splitting is noticed in the second G(r) peak of the HEMG after heat treatment. These changes observed in G(r) suggest a significant short- and medium-range structural change, which is quite different from that of the typical structural relaxation. As for the S(Q) (Fig. 1e), slight peak position shifting and sharpening of the first peak can be observed with a clearer splitting in the second peak, which reflects a structural ordering of the short- and medium-range structures as well. Synchrotron small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) experiments are further performed and confirm the amorphous structure (Supplementary Note 4 and Supplementary Fig. 13). cited_evidence.kind: web:The glass-to-glass transition and the glass structures of the HEMG
cited_evidence.text: During isothermal annealing experiments, the amorphous structure of the heat-treated sample remains stable after annealed at Tg – 5 K (759 K) for 2 h and even at Tg + 30 K (794 K) for 2 or 10 h (Supplementary Note 5 and Supplementary Fig. 14), respectively, which demonstrates the excellent thermal stability of the low-energy MG. Based on these results, an irreversible glass-to-glass transition from a high-energy HEMG (the as-prepared sample) to a low-energy HEMG (the heat-treated sample) is discovered, which is accompanied by an enormous heat release and a significant short- and medium-range structural change.

proposals.material_system: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy similar to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 in the amorphous (melt-spun ribbon) state
proposals.intervention: Apply a deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) to the as-quenched amorphous alloy
proposals.conditions: Expose the amorphous ribbons to liquid nitrogen temperatures (77 K) for 12 hours followed by a controlled warm-up to room temperature under an inert atmosphere
proposals.structural_mediator: Reduction of free volume and enhanced short-range atomic ordering
proposals.mechanism: DCT is expected to relieve residual internal stresses and initiate atomic rearrangements that lower the free volume, thereby inhibiting heterogeneous nucleation sites that could trigger crystallization upon subsequent heating
proposals.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy should display an increased glass transition temperature and a higher onset of crystallization (wider supercooled liquid region) relative to untreated, rapidly quenched samples, indicating improved glass-forming ability and thermal stability
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: A single-step DCT process does not presuppose a compound class and directly targets the amorphous structure to stabilize it thermally by promoting a denser, more homogeneous atomic configuration, which further prevents crystallization

proposals.material_system: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy using the CrMnFeCoNiP family (akin to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20) prepared via arc melting and rapid quenching
proposals.intervention: Introduce a minor microalloying addition of boron (e.g., 1 at% B, replacing a similar fraction of a base element)
proposals.conditions: Synthesize the modified alloy by arc melting with boron under a protective atmosphere followed by rapid melt spinning to achieve the amorphous state
proposals.mechanism: Boron has a strong affinity for phosphorus, promoting covalent-like bonding that encourages the formation of stable, dense atomic clusters. These clusters can interrupt the long-range atomic ordering necessary for crystallization, thereby enhancing thermal stability
proposals.predicted_outcome: The boron-doped alloy should show a higher critical cooling rate for glass formation, an expanded supercooled liquid region in DSC measurements, and delayed crystallization relative to a baseline undoped phosphorus-containing alloy
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By introducing an appropriate microalloying element, this single intervention steers the local chemistry towards forming inherently stable clusters that both improve the glass-forming ability and stabilize the amorphous state thermally without resorting to compound classes beyond elemental additions

proposals.material_system: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy, for instance, Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 in its as-quenched amorphous state
proposals.intervention: Subject the as-quenched alloy to a controlled sub–glass transition (sub-Tg) annealing treatment
proposals.conditions: Heat the amorphous sample to approximately 0.8×Tg (based on baseline DSC data) for one hour under an inert atmosphere and then quench to room temperature
proposals.structural_mediator: Enhanced medium-range ordering and relaxation of atomic configurations
proposals.mechanism: Sub-Tg annealing encourages subtle atomic rearrangements without triggering full crystallization. This structural relaxation reduces internal free volume and potential nucleation sites, thereby stabilizing the amorphous structure thermally
proposals.predicted_outcome: DSC measurements should reveal an upward shift in the crystallization onset temperature and a broader supercooled liquid region, while XRD and TEM analyses continue to confirm an amorphous structure compared to the unannealed baseline
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This single heat-treatment intervention is designed to kinetically stabilize the amorphous phase by optimizing the short- and medium-range order, directly addressing the need for improved glass-forming ability and thermal stability

proposals.material_system: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy (akin to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20) fabricated via rapid quenching into an amorphous state
proposals.intervention: Utilize an in situ pulsed laser remelting process immediately after melt-spinning
proposals.conditions: Expose the amorphous ribbon to short-duration (nanosecond-scale) high-energy laser pulses in a controlled, inert atmosphere; laser fluence and pulse repetition rate must be optimized to induce localized thermal remelting without complete crystallization
proposals.structural_mediator: Nano-scale atomic rearrangement and homogenization of residual free volume
proposals.mechanism: The pulsed laser treatment provides localized energy that encourages a controlled transient remelting of the amorphous matrix. This facilitates further atomic diffusion and homogenization, eliminating minor heterogeneities and free-volume pockets that serve as precursors for crystallization
proposals.predicted_outcome: Post-treatment, the alloy should demonstrate improved thermal stability evidenced by a higher crystallization onset temperature in DSC and a more uniform amorphous structure in TEM, compared to untreated rapidly quenched samples
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This intervention leverages a single processing step to modify the as-quenched glass structure on a nanoscopic scale. It directly reduces nucleation sites for crystallization, thereby enhancing both the glass-forming ability and thermal stability without changing the alloy composition

decision.rationale: Direction A directly targets the challenge by using a controlled sub–glass transition temperature (sub-Tg) annealing treatment to induce an irreversible glass-to-glass transition in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys. The approach leverages evidence from prior work (e.g., PMC9023469) where such heat treatments led to enhanced medium-range atomic ordering and improved thermal stability without inducing crystallization. The treatment parameters (heating to ~0.8×Tg for one hour under an inert atmosphere, then quenching) are clearly defined, which makes the process directly testable compared to the other proposals.
